title: Charlie Parker's unwritten notes: John Jackson blamed for missing parts
summary: Section mates keep telling Jackson he is missing notes until Dizzy sees Parker had been inventing parts not on the page.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: One of the things that I remember about this genius of Charlie Parker was.... Back to the time when we first rehearsed the band in New York, at our very first rehearsal, these arrangements we played, the eight arrangements that we played... And they had a good sound and everything, and the band was sounding good.

So later, after Charlie leaves the band and John Jackson came in the band, he was doing fine, you know. As any new member in the band, everybody would compliment them and try to give them little hints about things that were happening. So every night, when we would finish playing, someone would say to John Jackson something to the effect of, 'Hey man, you sure sounded great tonight. But in Number 22, in Letter E, there's a little thing in there, and it goes something like his.' And

he says, "Oh, I must have missed it, but I'll catch up on it." Then another night, a person would come in and say, "Yeah, like in the first chorus of such-and-such a thing," there's that little thing... After that, someone would say something else.

So after John Jackson is in the band about two weeks, somebody's still talking about these things that aren't happening. So somebody happened to mention it one night, and John had had a couple of drinks. And he flew into a rage. He said, "Dammit, I'm playin' everything I see! So I don't know what the hell you all are talkin' about. Hell, I've been here two weeks and I know I can read. What the hell is goin' on?"

Dizzy's in there, and Dizzy said, "What's the matter?" He said, "Man, they keep tellin' me about what I'm not playin' here, what I'm not playin' there. And I know I'm playin' everything I see." So Dizzy said, "That's all right. Man, we'll have a rehearsal tomorrow and straighten it out." And he told the rest of the guys, "Get off the cat's back, man." So the guys said, "Well, we're not on his back. We're just trying to help him along." "You're not helping me, man, because I'm playing everything I see."
So the next day, we rehearse these particular numbers, and we get to a certain part, and Dizzy would stop him... He'd say, "Okay, stop the band." And he'd ask John Jackson, "What

do you have right there?" And John Jackson would just take the music and hand it to Dizzy. And Dizzy looked at it, and he'd say "That dirty son-of-a-bitch." Everybody said, "What's happening." And what was learned was that from the very beginning, Charlie had been playing the part, adding what he wanted to in there, and just kept playing -- and nobody ever knew that it wasn't there. Charlie was playing things all through the arrangements that wasn't written at all. And John Jackson didn't do this. And everybody apologized to John, of course -- and it was a big laugh in the band.

But that's the kind of guy that Charlie was, that in these arrangements those kind of things were never heard really... Of course, the band never recorded with Charlie, so it couldn't have been heard.
